checkpoints: Unwrapping a DEK means sending the wrapped key to a KMS like Vault Transit and getting the plaintext key back over HTTP — each unwrap is a full network round-trip, not a local operation.

Calling `TransitService.unwrapDek` on every single read means the same record's DEK gets re-unwrapped from Vault on every request, even when it was just decrypted moments earlier, so the KMS round-trip dominates read latency.

Looping over N rows and `await`-ing `unwrapDek` inside the loop sequentially turns a batch/list endpoint into an N+1 pattern against the KMS: N records cost N separate HTTP round-trips whose latencies stack up one after another.

Putting the KMS directly on the hot read path also makes it a single point of failure for reads — if Vault slows down or becomes unreachable, every read request fails along with it, not just the writes that actually need fresh key material.

Caching the unwrapped DEK in memory for a short TTL (for example a `Map` keyed by wrapped DEK or record id storing `{ dek, expiresAt }`) lets repeat reads of the same record skip the Vault round-trip entirely until the entry expires.

The DEK cache must live only in process memory and never be written to disk, so a crash or restart loses it exactly as if it had never been cached — this preserves envelope-encryption's bounded blast radius and crypto-shredding guarantees, since the plaintext key never becomes durable outside Vault.

Fixing the N+1 in the batch endpoint means collecting all the wrapped DEKs and sending them in a single request to Vault Transit's batch endpoint (using a `batch_input` array) instead of issuing one `unwrapDek` call per row — this collapses N round-trips into one.

Running Vault Transit in high availability, such as multiple nodes behind a load balancer or Enterprise performance replicas, removes the single-node-failure risk so one Vault instance going down doesn't take every read with it, and the fix should be validated by comparing round-trip counts and p50/p99 read latency before and after, plus a test confirming the DEK cache actually expires at its TTL and is never persisted outside memory.
